Analysis.object: Self-conceptions and negative affect variables did not explain a significant amount of the variance in muscle dysmorphia symptoms. Muscle dysmorphia symptoms did account for a significant amount of variance in the sets of self-conception and negative affect variables. The relationship with muscle dysmorphia symptoms was stronger for the set of negative affect variables than the set of self-conceptions. The multivariate relationships with muscle dysmorphia symptoms were significant for Females in addition to males.

ATLAS and ATHENA programs may have benefited had they addressed muscle dysmorphia as a whole, rather than targeting steroid use in isolation. More specifically, our findings suggest that negative affect is more a consequence of, rather than a precursor to, muscle dysmorphia. Thus, a better choice in terms of intervention might be to treat muscle dysmorphia directly rather than depression as occurred within the ATHENA program. Our findings also support the continued development of interventions for both Female and male and tailoring these separate interventions according to gender-specific findings.

Population.object: Students were recruited from a Fast Fitness class or a Weight training class
